evidence.title: Social Remittances and Financial Remittances
evidence.author: Escribà-Folch, Abel; Meseguer, Covadonga; Wright, Joseph
excerpts: This chapter expounds on social remittances and financial remittances.

Advancements in information and communication technologies (ICT) have rendered the physical distance separating migrant families less relevant due to numerous digital alternatives to in-person meetings, such as international calls and international over-the-top (OTT) communication services.
Migrants simultaneously send their financial remittances and their experiences of beliefs and politics to their relatives back home.
Thus, social remittances could impact political behaviors such as increasing protest and decreasing electoral support.
On the other hand, political remittances are dependent whether emigration is politically motivated or driven by economic necessity.
Moreover, political conversations seemed to amplify the effect of monetary remittances on autocracy protests.

evidence.title: Influence of Remittances on Socio-Economic Development in Rural Nepal
evidence.author: Chaudhary, Deepak
excerpts: This article analyses socioeconomic changes with reference to income, consumption, expenditure, health, and education of migrant households in relation to remittances flows.
This study is based on a case study of Musaharniya village in Rajbiraj Municipality of Saptari District, Province 2, Nepal.
It is found that remittances play a vital role in improving the socioeconomic condition, reducing poverty and bringing social and political awareness in the village.
Those households whose family members are not abroad are poorer than those with migrant members abroad.
Due to increasing incomes, their expenditure capacity has considerably risen over time.
All migrant households have owned land whereas one-third of households were landless in the past.
Access to modern technologies has significantly increased among remittance recipient households compared to non-remittances households.
Remittances were also causing migration from rural to urban centres to some extent.

evidence.title: Nepal
excerpts: Nepal, officially Federal Democratic of Republic Nepal is a landlocked country in South Asia.
It is mainly situated in the Himalayas, but also includes parts of the Indo-Gangetic Plain.

It borders the Tibet Autonomous Region of China to the north, and India to the south, east, and west, while it is narrowly separated from Bangladesh by the Siliguri Corridor, and from Bhutan by the Indian state of Sikkim.

Nepal has a diverse geography, including fertile plains, subalpine forested hills, and eight of the world's ten highest mountains, including Mount Everest, the highest point above mean sea level on Earth.
Nepal is a multi-ethnic, multi-lingual, multi-religious, and multi-cultural sovereign state, with Nepali as the official language.

Parts of northern Nepal were intertwined with the culture of Tibet; that of the centrally located Kathmandu Valley is intertwined with the culture of Indo-Aryans, which was the seat of the prosperous Newar confederacy known as Nepal Mandala.
The Himalayan branch of the ancient Silk Road was dominated by the valley's traders.
The cosmopolitan region developed distinct traditional art and architecture.

By the 18th century, the Gorkha Kingdom had unified Nepal under the Shah dynasty, which established the Kingdom of Nepal and later formed an alliance with the British Empire under the Rana dynasty of premiers.
The country was never colonised but served as a buffer state between Imperial China and British India following the treaty of Sugauli.
Parliamentary democracy was introduced in 1951 but was twice suspended by Nepalese monarchs, in 1960 and 2005.
The Nepalese Civil War in the 1990s and early 2000s ended with the establishment of a secular republic in 2008, ending the world's last Hindu monarchy.

evidence.title: Anglo-Nepalese War
excerpts: The Anglo-Nepalese War (1 November 1814 – 4 March 1816), also known as the Anglo-Gorkha War, was a major military conflict fought between the Kingdom of Nepal and the East India Company (EIC).
The war was the culmination of decades of geopolitical friction as two expanding powers clashed along an ill-defined 1,500-kilometer frontier.
While Nepal had aggressively expanded its empire from the Teesta River in the east to the Sutlej River in the west, the EIC was simultaneously extending its dominion across the Indian subcontinent.
The initial conflicts were driven by competition over the fertile Tarai lowlands and trans-Himalayan trade routes into Tibet.
The final crisis emerged in May 1814 CE (Jeth 1871 BS), when a small Nepalese force attacked EIC police outposts in the disputed Butwal region, killing 18 EIC officials.
Citing this attack as a casus belli, Lord Hastings, the Governor-General of India, formally declared war on the Kingdom of Nepal on 1 November 1814 CE (18 Kartik 1871 BS).
The immediate catalyst for the war was a protracted territorial dispute over the border districts of Butwal and Sheoraj.
Following Nepal's annexation of the Kingdom of Palpa in 1806 CE (1863 BS), Nepal laid claim to these lowland dependencies.
However, the EIC asserted its own sovereignty over the region, having acquired the neighboring Oudh State territories from the Nawab of Awadh in 1801 CE (1858 BS).
After years of diplomatic deadlock, EIC forces occupied the disputed lands in early 1814 CE (1871 BS).
This provocation prompted the Nepalese to launch the retaliatory attack on EIC outposts later that year, triggering the war later that year.

Nepal fought the war entirely isolated; attempts by Bhimsen Thapa, the Mukhtiyar of the Kingdom of Nepal, to forge anti-British alliances with the Maratha Empire, the Sikh Empire, and Qing China ultimately failed.

evidence.title: India–Nepal relations
excerpts: The relationship between the two nations of India and Nepal is often known as Roti-Beti ka Rishta.

The Nepalese Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal describes the bilateral relation as

"We're not merely neighbours on the map; we're children of the same rivers"

evidence.title: Remittances to Nepal
excerpts: Remittances to Nepal are money transfers from Nepalese workers employed outside the country to friends or relatives in Nepal and form part of the wider global remittance transfers by migrant workers back to their home countries.
Remittances constitute a substantial economic pillar for Nepal.
In 2023, these inward transfers were valued at an estimated US$11 billion, contributing a significant 26.6% to the nation's gross domestic product.
This surpasses the aggregate inflow from both official development assistance and foreign direct investment, underscoring the critical role of remittances in Nepal's economic landscape.
It is said that remittances represented more than 20 percent of GDP in Nepal in the year 2017 onwards.
Moreover, it would be highly beneficial to the country, where there are natural calamities, political conflict, people war, low investment in entrepreneurial activities and economic recession.
In the financial year (FY) 2000/01, the banking sector showed that NPR 15.9 billion was received.
Remittances to Nepal are facilitated by numerous remittance companies operating through global partner networks.
